title: Draw near to God (James 4:1–10)
hook: draw near to God and he will draw near to you

segments.voice: Yesterday, wisdom from above, gentle and easy to be intreated, and your line was gentle wisdom.

"From whence come wars and fightings among you?" That's how James opens chapter four, in the King James Bible, and he isn't talking about armies. He means the believers he's writing to. Arguments in the parking lot. Grudges that last for years. Where does all that come from? It's a fair question for any family, any office, any group chat that's gone quiet and cold. James's answer is uncomfortable, and then, a few lines later, it turns into a promise.

Here's his answer: "come they not hence, even of your lusts that war in your members?" The fight outside starts as a fight inside. You want something and don't have it, so you scheme and quarrel. Then a short line that stings: "ye have not, because ye ask not." Or you ask with the wrong motives, just to spend it on your own pleasures. Then James quotes Proverbs: "God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble." And the letter turns. A string of short commands, almost like a drumbeat. "Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you." Some readers hear a priestly word in draw nigh: the old Greek translation of Exodus uses it for priests who come near to the Lord. If so, James hands that priestly word to everyone. And the promise has two sides. You take a step, and God takes a step. In James's picture, God isn't waiting at a distance with crossed arms. God comes toward you. Then what drawing near looks like: wash your hands, purify your hearts, you double minded. Let your laughter turn to mourning, he says, meaning take your wrongs seriously. Then the last line lifts everything back up: "Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he shall lift you up." The fights start inside, and so does the way back.
screen: `YE HAVE NOT, BECAUSE YE ASK NOT.`

segments.voice: Picture a doorway, and you standing a few steps back from it, and name what has kept you at a distance lately: busyness, a quarrel, shame, or just forgetting. In your mind, take one step forward, toward God or toward the holy as you understand it, without fixing everything first, and imagine the other side of the promise: the doorway coming closer to you too. If you pray, you can simply say, here I am.
Double minded. James's name for the proud and quarreling: told to purify their hearts and draw near to God, who then draws near to them.
Your line: draw near. A promise with two sides. That's day six hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: Some churches use James 4:8 as a call to worship or before a prayer of confession, especially in Lent, when worshipers are invited to come near to God.

chat.says: James says draw nigh to God. What does he promise when you do?
options: That God draws near to you too: you take a step, and God takes one.
That you must cross the whole distance alone while God waits.
That you become a priest, allowed into the Temple's holy place.
chat.meaning: "Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you": in James's picture, God comes toward the one who comes near.
